props.title: Being 17
props.initialSlug: A love story that defies age

sections.content: **Being 17 (2016)** (2016) masterfully captures the raw intensity of adolescent awakening through the story of two feuding teenage boys in the French Pyrenees. Director André Téchiné, collaborating with writer Céline Sciamma (**Girlhood** (2014), **Portrait of a Lady on Fire** (2019)), creates a visceral coming-of-age narrative that recalls the emotional authenticity of **Show Me Love** (1998) and the charged tension of **My Beautiful Laundrette** (1985). The film's strength lies in its unflinching portrayal of how physical aggression masks deeper attractions.

sections.content: The film's exploration of masculinity and vulnerability connects to a rich tradition of European coming-of-age cinema, including **La vie d'Adèle** (2013) and **Wild Reeds** (1994) - the latter also directed by Téchiné. What sets **Being 17** apart is its focus on the physical - both in terms of the rugged mountain setting and the boys' aggressive interactions. The camera work emphasizes this physicality, with handheld shots that mirror the characters' restless energy.

The maternal figure played by Sandrine Kiberlain adds another layer of complexity, reminiscent of the family dynamics in **Mommy** (2014) and **I Killed My Mother** (2009). Her character serves as both catalyst and witness to the evolving relationship between the boys, creating a unique triangular dynamic rarely seen in coming-of-age films. sections.content: **Being 17** emerges from a strong contemporary wave of French LGBTQ+ cinema, alongside works like **BPM (Beats Per Minute)** (2017) and **Portrait of a Lady on Fire** (2019). These films share a commitment to depicting queer experiences with naturalistic authenticity rather than melodrama. The school setting of **Being 17** particularly resonates with films like **Jongens** (2014) and **Hidden Away** (2014), which similarly explore the intersection of academic and emotional education.
